rows.text: Genuinely smooth for a linear happy path. Creating the dossier, generating the five admin leaves in one action, uploading the bilingual PM/labelling, then validate-block-fix-re-validate-export all flowed without me guessing my next move. The one place I actually paused was the placeholder-to-real ID re-key, but the 409 told me exactly which finding to clear, so I never felt stuck the way I do fishing through docuBridge error logs.

Honestly easier than I expected for a first pass. Create dossier, see the 8 Module 1 leaves at 0/8, generate the five admin leaves, upload the bilingual PM and labelling with both EN and FR, and I'm at 100% placed without fighting the tool. The one moment of real friction — export blocked 409 on the placeholder ID — resolved itself in three obvious moves (REP request, Rename to the real ID, re-validate), and everything downstream just flowed. This is the smoothest a linear eCTD dry-run has felt for me outside Vault.

Genuinely smooth for someone who does this daily. Module 1 populated fast — five admin leaves tool-authored, PM/labelling uploaded bilingual with both EN and FR recognized, 8/8 in about ten minutes. The placeholder-ID block was the only real friction, and even that was a two-click fix (REP request, then Rename to the real ID). This is far less fiddly than hand-assembling folders and running eValidator round-trips in eCTD Office.

Genuinely smooth. Create dossier, generate the five admin leaves, upload the bilingual PM/labelling with both EN and FR, and Module 1 goes 0 to 100 without me fighting the tool. The placeholder-ID block was the only speed bump and even that was one Rename away from clearing. This is faster than assembling in eCTD Office by hand, and I didn't have to think about the backbone XML at all.

Honestly easier than I expected. The module checklist showed me all 8 required Module 1 docs up front with a 0/8 progress bar, the tool auto-authored 5 of the admin leaves for me, and I just uploaded the bilingual PM and labelling. The only real friction was the export getting blocked, but even then it told me exactly why and what to do, so I never felt stuck.

Honestly easier than I expected — I created the dossier, saw the 8-doc Module 1 checklist with a live 0/8 to 100% progress bar, let it generate the admin leaves and uploaded the bilingual PM/labelling, and every step told me where I stood. The one place I had to think was the placeholder-ID blocker, but the export error literally handed me the next action (file the REP request, then Rename to the real ID), so even as a junior I never got stuck. Sign, import-check, and the one preflight report were basically click-and-read.

Honestly easier than I expected for something this regulated. Create dossier, place the eight Module 1 leaves (five auto-generated, three uploaded with EN/FR), validate, export, sign — it was linear and each step told me exactly where I stood, right down to 8/8 100% and the 11008-byte zip. The one real speed bump, the placeholder-ID export block, was self-explanatory and I cleared it by filing the REP request and setting the real HC ID e478210. I wasn't guessing at any point.

Honestly, easier than I expected for something this regulated. Creating the dossier, generating the five admin leaves in one shot, and uploading the bilingual PM/labelling with both EN and FR files moved me from 0/8 to 8/8 without me having to guess at the Module 1 structure. The one real snag — the export getting slammed with a 409 — turned out to be well-signposted, and the placeholder-to-real Dossier ID rename cleared it cleanly. I got all the way to a signed, exported, hand-off-ready package, so the path itself is linear and doable.

Genuinely smooth for a task that usually chews up my day. Seventeen steps and the only real friction was the placeholder-ID block, which is exactly the friction I want — it stopped me instead of letting me ship garbage. Generating the five admin leaves and getting Module 1 to 8/8 took minutes, not the back-and-forth I run in eValidator plus my own checklists. Nothing hidden, nothing I had to reverse-engineer.

Genuinely smooth, and I say that as someone who does this by hand with eValidator and a stack of checklists. Create dossier, generate the five admin leaves, upload the bilingual PM and labelling with both EN and FR, validate, hit the block, file the REP request, rename to the real ID, re-validate, export, sign — it was linear and every step landed where I expected. The only real friction was cognitive: I had to keep straight that the placeholder-ID block was the ONLY thing stopping me, and that the ten PDF/A items were advisory-only — the report told me that, but a first-timer might panic at "10 warnings."

Genuinely smooth for a first-timer with zero reg background. Create dossier, generate the 5 admin leaves, upload the bilingual PM/labelling, and Module 1 hit 100% without me guessing what belonged where. The only real thinking was the placeholder-to-real Dossier ID rename, but the block told me exactly what to do, so I never got stuck. Maybe an hour of clicking versus the weeks of consultant back-and-forth I'm used to.

Honestly smoother than I expected for something this regulated. Twelve-ish meaningful clicks to a signed, exported, self-checked package — that's a lot faster than the back-and-forth with my consultancy.

Genuinely smooth for someone who publishes daily — the linear path (create, place Module 1, validate, hit the block, fix, re-validate, export, attest, sign, self-check, report) mapped exactly to how I actually work a sequence. The one honest bit of friction is the placeholder-to-real Dossier ID via Rename, but the block told me precisely what to do, so I never guessed. Generating the five admin leaves and getting the bilingual 1.3.1/1.3.3 to accept both EN and FR without fighting me is faster than my current PM-into-docuBridge dance.

Honestly, this went smoothly for a first hands-on pass. Create dossier, generate the five admin leaves, upload the bilingual PM and labelling, validate, hit the block, re-key the Dossier ID, re-validate, export — the path was linear and I never had to guess where I was. The one bit of real-world friction is that I still have to leave the tool to actually file the REP request and run eValidator, but that's honest, not a defect. As a publisher I could get a clean sequence out in one sitting.

Honestly easier than I expected for something this regulated. Honestly easier than I expected for something this regulated. Honestly easier than I expected — the Module 1 checklist mapped exactly to the 8 leaves I know, and the split between tool-generated admin leaves and my upload-only bilingual PM/labelling (1.3.1, 1.3.3, both EN+FR) matched how I actually work. The one thing that could have thrown me — the placeholder Dossier ID blocking export — was self-explaining: it told me to file the REP request and Rename to the real ID, and after that it just flowed to a clean export.

Honestly smoother than I expected. Generating the five admin leaves in one shot and only uploading the bilingual PM and labelling myself is exactly how I think about Module 1 — the tool did the tedious admin authoring and left me the two documents that are genuinely mine. The placeholder-to-real Dossier ID re-key with content carrying over was painless, and I never had to fight the interface. The only "work" was the two upload steps and setting the real ID, which is right.

Honestly, easier than I braced for. It was a straight line — create the dossier, place the eight Module 1 leaves, validate, hit the wall, fix the ID, re-validate, export, sign. The steps came in the order I'd actually work them, and the placeholder-ID block wasn't a mystery — it told me plainly to file the REP request and set the real ID. For a paper-and-Word man like me, the only real friction was trusting the generated admin leaves, but they were mine to review, so I got through it without calling anyone.

Honestly, easier than I feared for a man who still keeps printed binders. It was a straight line: make the dossier, generate the admin leaves, upload my PM and labelling in both languages, validate, hit the wall, fix the ID, re-validate, export, sign. The only real head-scratcher was the placeholder-ID business, but the block spelled out exactly what to do, so I never felt lost or stuck guessing.

Genuinely smooth. Create dossier, generate the 5 admin leaves, upload the bilingual PM/labelling, validate, hit the block, file the REP request, rename to the real ID, re-validate, export, attest, sign, self-check, pull the report — it was a clean linear path with no dead ends. The one place I had to actually do something was clearing the placeholder-ID block, and the fix was obvious because the error told me exactly what to do.

Honestly easier than I expected for a first hands-on pass. Create dossier, generate the five admin leaves, upload the bilingual PM/labelling, validate, export — it moved linearly and the module progress (0/8 -> 5/8 -> 8/8) told me exactly where I stood. The one place I braced for pain, the export, actually helped me: the 409 named the exact blocker and told me what to do, so I re-keyed to the real Dossier ID and it cleared in one pass. As a CDMO manager who lives in Freyr, this is a smooth Module 1 flow.

Honestly easier than I feared going in with zero eCTD background. The path was linear and each step had a single obvious next action: eight required Module 1 leaves listed, five auto-authored, three uploaded, then validate. Hitting the 409 export block on the placeholder ID could have stalled me, but it named the exact fix (file the REP request, set the real Dossier ID), so I recovered without guessing.

Honestly easier than I feared for someone who's never touched eCTD. The module builder handed me a plain 8-item checklist, auto-authored the five admin leaves from details I'd already entered, and I only had to upload the PM and labelling PDFs. The one place I stalled was the export 409 block, but it named the exact rule and told me what to do, so I wasn't guessing. Signing and pulling the final report took a couple of clicks each.

Very clear at every step. Module 1 showed 8/8 with real progress percentages, the validator returned actual CA-REP-0001 rule IDs rather than vague red text, and the export block named the exact blocker instead of handing me a broken zip. The distinction between a recorded eValidator PASS (cleared=false) and PASS-plus-attached-report (cleared=true) was unusually well drawn — that is precisely the nuance my juniors get wrong.

Very clear at every step, which is not what I'm used to. The validation report gave me a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and a plain-language cause — placeholder ID — not a cryptic code I have to look up. The 409 export block told me exactly which finding was stopping me and what to do, and the eValidator flow was explicit that a bare PASS isn't CLEARED until I attach the actual report file, which is precisely the distinction my team gets wrong. Only nuance: the difference between the tool's own structural validator and HC's official eValidator has to be read carefully, but to their credit the disclaimer is stated everywhere.

Very clear at every step. The validator told me exactly one blocker with a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and separated it from the 10 advisory-only PDF/A notes, so I knew instantly it was placeholder-ID, not a content problem. The 409 export block named the exact finding instead of handing me a broken zip, and the re-validate flipped to PASS with 0 errors. No guessing about what the system wanted.

Very clear at every step. The validation report gave me real rule IDs (CA-REP-0001) not vague red text, and it told me plainly the 10 PDF/A items were advisory-only and never block. The 409 export block named the exact finding instead of handing me a broken zip. The evalidator flow was honest that a bare PASS isn't CLEARED until I attach the actual report file — that distinction is exactly right and I understood it immediately.

Very clear at almost every step. The placeholder-ID banner warned me early, and when validation came back NOT PASSED it named the exact rule (CA-REP-0001) in plain language instead of a cryptic code. The one spot I had to slow down and read was the eValidator flow — a bare "pass" attestation didn't clear it, I had to also attach the actual report file to reach CLEARED — but the messages explained the difference, so I got there.

Very clear at almost every step — the validation report gave me an actual rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and a plain-English message instead of a vague "not valid," which is exactly what I'd paste to a senior when I ask for help. The export block (HTTP 409) showing the exact blocking finding, then watching it flip to PASSED after I set the real ID, made cause-and-effect obvious. The only mild confusion was the two-step eValidator attestation (record pass -> cleared=False, then attach the report file -> cleared=True); I understand WHY now, but the first time "pass but not cleared" made me pause.

Very clear, and clear in the way I actually care about. When export failed it was a hard 409 with the exact rule CA-REP-0001 and plain-language instructions, not a silent broken download. The validation report named its version (v1.2, synced to HC criteria v5.3), listed what it checked and — critically — what it does NOT check. I never had to wonder what a green checkmark meant.

Very clear at every gate, which for me is the whole ballgame. When validation came back NOT PASSED it named the exact rule (CA-REP-0001), told me plainly it was just the placeholder ID, and separated that hard blocker from the 10 advisory-only PDF/A notes so I wasn't chasing phantom problems. The 409 export block even echoed the blocking finding and the fix, and the preflight report at the end laid out structural, eValidator, signature, and REP status in one object with the next step spelled out. I never once had to wonder what the system was telling me.

Very clear at every step, and clear in the way that matters to a former screener: the validator gave me a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001) with a plain-language fix and told me the 10 PDF/A items were advisory-only, not blockers — that distinction is where I've watched sponsors panic needlessly. The 409 export block named the exact finding instead of handing me a misleading zip. The one thing I'd want spelled out more is which specific leaves generated the 10 advisories, but the report told me they were the plain uploads, so I could live with it.

Very clear, and clearer than most vendor tools because it names the actual rule ID — CA-REP-0001, placeholder_dossier_id — instead of a vague "not ready." The 409 export block spelled out the exact remediation (file through REP, then Rename to the issued ID), which is precisely the sequence I'd tell a client. The one thing I'd watch: the two-step eValidator flow (attest pass, THEN attach the report to reach CLEARED) is correct behavior but non-obvious — I only understood why cleared stayed False after reading the note that a bare pass isn't evidence.

Very clear at each step. The validator gave me a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and a plain-English fix, not a cryptic code; the 409 export block spelled out the exact blocking finding instead of handing me a broken download. The distinction between "attestation recorded" (cleared=False) and "report attached" (cleared=True) was a little subtle but honestly correct, and the preflight report tied everything into one picture I could actually read.

Very clear at every step, which matters because I have zero regulatory background. The validation report gave me an actual rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and a plain-English cause — placeholder ID — not some cryptic code I'd have to email someone about. The one thing I stumbled on was that a recorded eValidator PASS wasn't enough — it stayed cleared=false until I attached the actual report file; that surprised me for a second, but honestly it's the right call and the message told me exactly what was missing.

At every step I knew what the system was telling me. The validation report used real CA-<severity>-<block> rule IDs (CA-REP-0001), separated the one hard blocker from the 10 advisory PDF/A warnings, and named the exact remediation — that is the language I live in. The 409 fail-closed export with the blocking finding echoed back, and the X-Export-Validation='passed' header on the successful zip, are exactly the signals I check for.

Very clear at every step. The validation report gave me actual CA-<severity>-<block> rule IDs (CA-REP-0001), separated the one hard blocker from the 10 advisory-only PDF/A notes, and told me exactly why — placeholder ID, file through REP, then Rename. The 409 on export named the finding instead of handing me a bad download, which is exactly how a fail-closed publisher should behave. I always knew what the system was telling me and what to do next.

At every step I knew what the system was telling me and what to do next. The 0/8 to 8/8 module progress, the NOT PASSED report with one blocker plus 10 advisory-only PDF/A notes clearly flagged as non-blocking, and the 409 export block showing the exact finding instead of handing me a broken zip — none of that left me guessing. The distinction between "recorded pass" and "CLEARED once the report is attached" was a little subtle, but the messages spelled it out. I'd have zero trouble explaining any of this to a filer or to my own management.

Very clear at every gate. The validation report gave me an actual rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and a plain-English reason — placeholder ID needs the real HC Dossier ID — instead of a vague "not ready." The 409 export block repeated the exact finding rather than handing me a misleading download, and the PASS after the rename was unambiguous. The only thing I'd have to learn is the distinction between "attested pass" and "CLEARED with report attached," but the screen spelled that out too.

Very clear at every step. The validation report gave me a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and told me plainly it was the placeholder ID, not a vague red X, and it separated the 10 PDF/A items as advisory-only so I didn't panic that my uploaded PMs were broken. The 409 export block naming the exact finding, and the distinction between a recorded eValidator PASS versus the CLEARED state only after I attached the actual report — that precision is the language my QA people speak.

Very clear at every step. Progress showed 0/8, then 5/8, then 8/8, and the validation report named the exact blocker as CA-REP-0001 with plain-language guidance — file through REP, then Rename to the real ID. The 409 export block didn't leave me guessing; it showed me the finding instead of a fake download. As a bilingual PM person I especially liked seeing 1.3.1 and 1.3.3 confirm BOTH EN and FR attached — that's the thing that usually bites us.

Very clear, and that's the part that surprised me. Every screen told me exactly where I stood — 0/8, then 5/8, then 8/8, then a validation report with a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and a plain-English reason, not a cryptic code. When export got blocked with a 409, it didn't just fail — it showed me the one finding and the exact next step. I always knew what the system was telling me and what it wanted from me next.

Very clear, and that surprised me. Module 1 showed all 8 required leaves with a running 0/8 to 8/8 count, so I always knew what was still missing. When export failed it said 409 'validation_not_passed' and named the one finding, CA-REP-0001, in plain English — file the REP request, set the real ID, rename. No mystery codes, no dead ends.

At every step I knew what the system was telling me. The validator gave me a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001) with a plain-language fix, the 409 export block named the exact blocker instead of dumping a broken zip, and the CLEARED state only lit up after I attached the actual report file, not just a bare pass. Nothing was ambiguous, and the disclaimers rode inline so I never had to guess what a green check actually meant.

Very clear throughout. Every step showed me what to do next and the system told me why — the validator returned a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001) with a plain-language fix, not a cryptic code, and it separated the one blocking error from the 10 advisory PDF/A warnings so I wasn't chasing noise. The eValidator flow was the sharpest: it explicitly told me a bare PASS wasn't enough (cleared=False) until I attached the actual report file, then flipped to CLEARED. I never had to guess what state my filing was in.

Very clear. The validator told me exactly what was blocking (CA-REP-0001, placeholder ID) versus what was merely advisory (the 10 PDF/A notes that never block), which is precisely the distinction I would have panicked over on my own. The progress counter (0/8 -> 5/8 -> 8/8), the rule IDs, and the plain-language next-step text meant I always knew where I stood and what the system was telling me.

Very clear at nearly every step. The placeholder-ID banner up front warned me the d4821 wasn't real before I got burned by it, and when export blocked with CA-REP-0001 the message literally spelled out "file a Dossier ID Request through REP, then set the real ID (Rename)." The distinction between a recorded eValidator pass and the CLEARED state (which needs the actual report attached) was subtle but the labels made it obvious why I wasn't done yet.

This earned more trust than I expected, mostly because of its honesty. It fails closed on export, it stamps X-Export-Validation=passed, it never once claims to BE Health Canada's eValidator, and it labels the eValidator result as user-attested-external with the disclaimer travelling on the object. The maintained criteria-sync trail (v1.2, next review 2026-08) tells me it is not a stale one-time snapshot. I would trust it as a structural pre-flight and QA hand-off layer — I would NOT, and it correctly does not ask me to, treat it as a substitute for running the real eValidator before transmission.

This earned more trust than anything I've trialed in a while, precisely because it refuses to overclaim. It failed closed on the placeholder ID instead of handing me a downloadable-but-invalid package, it was blunt that the REP request is recorded but transmitted=False, and it never once pretended its structural check was Health Canada's eValidator — it kept telling me to run the real one before transmitting. The criteria-sync provenance (v1.2, synced to HC v5.3, quarterly review, append-only changelog) is exactly the maintenance evidence I'd need to defend using it to a client. I would trust it as a pre-flight and QA hand-off layer; I would not — and it agrees — treat it as the final gate before transmission.

This earns real trust precisely because it doesn't overclaim. It fails closed — refused to export on a placeholder ID — and it repeatedly, explicitly says it is NOT HC's eValidator and that eValidator is user-attested, not something it ran or verified. The maintained criteria trail (v1.2 synced to HC v5.3, quarterly review) tells me the ruleset isn't a stale snapshot. I would rely on it as a structural pre-flight, never as a substitute for the official eValidator run on the exported package — and it tells me that itself.

This earns real trust because it's honest about its edges. It fails closed on export, it labels its validator as structural-only and NOT HC's eValidator, it records the REP request but tells me straight that transmitted=False, and it treats my external eValidator result as user-attested evidence it doesn't reproduce. The SSO-verified signer with segregation-of-duties separation on an immutable Part-11 manifest is what an auditor actually wants. I'd still run the real eValidator before transmit — which is exactly what it tells me to do — but I'd rely on this to get me to a clean, defensible package.

This is what won me over. It fails closed — it flat refused to export a package while validation hadn't passed (409), so it can't hand me a misleading download. And it's honest about its own limits everywhere: it says outright it is NOT Health Canada's official eValidator, that the REP request is recorded but not transmitted, and that the eValidator PASS is my own attested evidence. For someone still learning HC terminology, that honesty makes me trust it MORE, not less — as long as I still run the real eValidator before transmitting, which it keeps telling me to do.

I'd trust it as a structural pre-flight, not as the final word — and that's exactly what it keeps telling me, which is why I trust it MORE. It fails closed (won't emit a package until validation truly passes), stamps the export "passed" with 0 missing leaves, and on every screen it says in plain language "this is NOT Health Canada's official eValidator — run eValidator before you transmit." The criteria-sync history (v1.2, synced to HC v5.3, next review dated) reassured me the ruleset isn't stale, and the Part-11 signature with a separate SSO-verified approver is the kind of audit trail my seniors would actually check. It's honest about not transmitting the REP request, which as someone still learning the terminology makes me trust it rather than fear I'm being misled.

This is where it earned real credibility with me. It fails closed — it refused to emit a package until validation genuinely passed — and it never once pretended to be Health Canada's eValidator; every screen repeated that this is a structural check and I must run the official eValidator before transmitting. The eValidator step was honest to a fault: a bare attested PASS was NOT enough, it demanded the actual report file before it would say CLEARED. And the Part-11 signature was SSO-verified with a real issuer, segregation-of-duties enforced, durable on a tamper-evident manifest that survived read-back. I would trust this to PREPARE and QA a real filing; I would still run HC's own eValidator myself, which is exactly what it tells me to do.

This earned more trust than any regulated tool I've trialed, precisely because it refuses to overclaim. It fails closed — no package comes out until validation genuinely passes — and it repeats, everywhere, that its checker is structural-only and is NOT Health Canada's eValidator, that the REP request is recorded but NOT transmitted, and that the eValidator PASS is user-attested, not something it ran. The criteria-sync trail (v1.2, synced to HC v5.3, quarterly review, versioned changelog) tells me the ruleset is maintained, not a stale snapshot. That said, I'd still verify the Part-11 claims myself — the SSO-verified signer, segregation-of-duties separation, and tamper-evident manifest all read right, but for a real filing my sign-off requires I test the audit trail's immutability and the signature-verifies-against-current-leaves behavior with my own hands before I rely on it.

More than I expected to, precisely because it never overclaims. It fails closed on export, the criteria carry a versioned sync trail against HC eCTD Criteria v5.3 with a review cadence, and every screen repeats that this is a structural check and NOT HC's eValidator — run the real one before you transmit. The REP request honestly says transmitted=False, the eValidator PASS isn't 'cleared' until the actual report file is attached, and the e-sign is SSO-verified with real segregation-of-duties separation. That honesty is what earns my trust — I'd rely on it as a pre-flight, never as a substitute for my own eValidator run, which is exactly how it positions itself.

This earned more trust than I expected, precisely because it refuses to overclaim. It fails closed on export, it stamps every result "structural only — NOT Health Canada's official eValidator," it says transmitted=False on the REP request instead of pretending it filed, and it treats my external eValidator PASS as user-attested evidence it did not reproduce. The versioned criteria-sync trail (v1.2, synced to HC v5.3, next review 2026-08) tells me the ruleset is maintained, not a stale snapshot. I would rely on it as a strong pre-flight to catch structural defects before I burn an eValidator run — I would NOT, and it explicitly agrees, treat its PASS as a substitute for the real eValidator or for HC screening.

This earned real trust because it kept telling me what it is NOT. It fails closed on export, it stamps every result as user-attested, and it repeats loudly that it is not HC's official eValidator and that REP requests are not transmitted. For a cost-driven founder that honesty is worth more than a fake green checkmark, because I know exactly where my consultant-level risk still lives. I'd trust it to get me structurally clean and hand-off-ready, not to be the final word before I transmit.

This is where it earned real credibility with me. It refused to emit a package while validation failed (fail-closed 409), it showed me the exact blocker, and it passed only after I genuinely fixed it — that's a tool that won't let me fool myself. What sells me is the relentless honesty: it says out loud "this is NOT Health Canada's eValidator," the REP request is "transmitted=false," and the eValidator PASS is "user-attested, we didn't run it." I'd trust it to get me structurally clean and hand-off-ready, but I understood clearly it does not replace the official eValidator run before transmit — which is exactly the boundary I need to know.

This earned more trust than anything I expected from a new tool, precisely because it refuses to overclaim. It fails closed on export, it distinguishes its own structural check from HC's eValidator in writing on every screen, and it treats my external eValidator PASS as user-attested — not cleared until I attach the actual report file. The SSO-verified signer with segregation-of-duties separation on an immutable Part-11 manifest, plus the criteria-sync provenance (v1.2, synced to HC v5.3, next review dated), is the auditable trail I need. I would still run real eValidator before transmit, but that is exactly what it tells me to do — so yes, I'd rely on it as the pre-flight, not the final word.

This earned real trust for what it claims to be — a structural pre-flight, not eValidator. The disclaimers are everywhere and correct: structural PDF/A-1b markers only (not full ISO 19005-1), user-attested external eValidator result it does not reproduce, REP prepared-but-not-transmitted, e-sign as Part-11-aligned tamper-evidence not a certification. The criteria-sync trail (v1.2, synced to HC v5.3, dated changelog, next review) tells me the ruleset is maintained, not a stale snapshot. I would rely on it to get a sequence structurally clean and to organize my Part-11 hand-off — but I'd still run HC's eValidator before transmit, which is exactly what it tells me to do, so the trust and the tool are aligned.

This earned more trust than most tools I've seen precisely because it refuses to overclaim. It fails closed on export, it stamps the eValidator result as user-attested and says plainly it did NOT run HC's eValidator, and it tells me the REP request is recorded but not transmitted. The maintained-criteria trail (v1.2, synced to HC v5.3, next review Aug) tells me the ruleset isn't a stale snapshot. I would rely on it as a pre-flight and QA hand-off gate — not as a substitute for the real eValidator, which it is the first to admit, and that honesty is exactly why I'd trust it for the real thing.
